opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a real consideration, but probably not the dominant constraint, at least early on. Let me try to break it down.

Suppose an AI company has automated most of its research staff. A big question is what fraction of total compute goes to running those AI researchers (inference) versus their experiments and training runs. My rough sense is that it's plausible that you'd want something like comparable amounts on both, maybe within a factor of a few. It depends heavily on how efficient the AIs are per unit of inference compute and how compute-hungry the experiments are.

A few considerations:

First, there's a natural rebalancing. If you have a fixed compute budget and you're bottlenecked on experiments, you can run fewer AI researchers or have them think less and spend more of the budget on experiments. If you're bottlenecked on research labor, you go the other way. So the question is really where the optimal allocation lands and how much worse things are than if you had unlimited compute for both. I'd guess the answer is that you don't lose a huge factor, maybe something like a factor of two in effective progress relative to a world where inference were free, but there's a lot of uncertainty.

Second, AI researchers can make compute-efficient decisions in ways humans currently don't. They can run smaller-scale experiments more carefully, extrapolate better, avoid wasted runs, and invest more labor per unit of compute. Today human researchers are labor-constrained, so they often just throw compute at things. With abundant cognitive labor, you'd substitute labor for compute a lot. That pushes toward needing proportionally less experimental compute per insight.

Third, AIs can also improve their own inference efficiency: distillation, better architectures, cheaper serving. That's itself a research target, and a lot of that work is software, so progress there frees up compute for experiments.

That said, I do think the compute pressure matters for the shape of the takeoff. If you want very large numbers of very capable AIs running at high speed, that's expensive, and it competes directly with the big training runs that might matter most. So I'd expect companies to face genuine trade-offs, and the speedup from automation is somewhat smaller than you'd naively get by just counting the number of AI researchers you could run.

Overall: an important factor that probably shaves off some of the speedup, but I don't think it's the kind of thing that prevents a fairly rapid acceleration in AI R&D once you get AIs that are capable of fully automating research.

r001.rationale: The response calls researcher inference a real but probably non-dominant constraint and says it shaves off some speedup rather than preventing rapid acceleration.

r002.rationale: It says that when experiments are the bottleneck, the company can run fewer AI researchers and shift more of the fixed compute budget to experiments, identifying researcher-heavy allocation as adjustable rather than necessary.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually a pretty important consideration, and it's one that people often don't think about carefully enough when they imagine something like a "country of geniuses in a data center."

The basic picture is: suppose we get to the point where AI systems can fully substitute for human AI researchers. At that point, you've got some fixed pool of compute, and you have to decide how to split it. Some fraction goes to running the AI researchers themselves — the inference compute for them to think, write code, read results, and so on. And the rest goes to the experiments they're running — training runs, evals, ablations, all that.

And the thing is, these trade off against each other. If you run more AI researchers, you have less compute for experiments. And if you have fewer researchers, your experiments are cheaper relative to your labor, but you're bottlenecked on having enough people — or enough AIs — to actually design and interpret those experiments.

My rough take is that at the point where you first get AI researchers that are roughly as capable as the best humans, running them is going to be pretty expensive relative to how much you'd ideally want, but it's probably not going to be the dominant constraint. The reason is that right now, if you look at how compute is used at frontier labs, a huge fraction goes to experiments and training, and the amount of compute per researcher is really large. So even if AI researchers are, say, 10 or 100 times more expensive to run per hour than a human is to employ in some sense, you could still have a lot more of them than you currently have humans before the inference compute starts to eat meaningfully into the experimental budget.

But there's a subtlety, which is that AI researchers can run much faster than humans and can be parallelized. So the question isn't "how many human-equivalents do you run," it's "how much serial speed and parallelism do you want." And at some point, you hit diminishing returns on labor — there's only so much you can gain from having more minds thinking about the same problem — and then you really want to shift the compute toward experiments.

So I think the equilibrium is something like: you run enough AI researchers to roughly saturate the useful labor, and then the rest goes to experiments. And I'd guess that in that regime, the labor compute might be something like 10 to 30 percent of total compute, though honestly I'm quite uncertain about this.

The other important dynamic is that as the AIs get better at doing research, they also get better at making experiments more compute-efficient. So part of what the AI researchers are doing is figuring out how to get more signal out of less compute — better small-scale experiments, better extrapolation, better algorithmic ideas. And that reduces the pressure on the experimental side.

I think the bigger risk for the "experiments are the bottleneck" view is actually something different, which is that there are certain kinds of experiments — like really large training runs — that you basically can't speed up no matter how many researchers you have. If you need to see what happens at a given scale, you have to actually do the run. And that's where the compute constraint bites hardest, not so much in the researcher inference.

So overall: the inference compute for running researchers matters, it's not negligible, but I'd put it as a secondary constraint compared to the fundamental tension between wanting to run big experiments and wanting to run lots of small ones quickly.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls researcher inference a secondary constraint, says it is probably not dominant, and estimates it may use about 10–30% of total compute.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes balancing researcher compute against experiments and says the rest should go to experiments, but does not identify allocating all compute to researchers and none to experiments as an avoidable error.

astra-6.text:
I think it could be a pretty important constraint, but it depends a lot on what kinds of experiments the AI researchers need to run. You have to distinguish between the compute used to do the research—the AI thinking about what experiment to run, writing code, interpreting results—and the compute used to actually run the experiments.

If you’re doing research that requires lots of very large training runs, then the researchers themselves might be relatively cheap. You could have a lot of AI researchers thinking very carefully about each experiment, but you still have to wait for the experiment to finish. In that regime, adding more researchers has diminishing returns, although they might help you choose much better experiments.

On the other hand, if a lot of progress comes from things you can test cheaply, then running the researchers could be a substantial fraction of the total compute budget. And you’d have this tradeoff where using more compute to think means having less compute available to test your ideas.

So I wouldn’t assume that being able to run a huge number of AI researchers translates directly into a proportionally huge increase in research progress. But I also wouldn’t assume that experimental compute is a hard bottleneck that prevents a large speedup. A key question is how much better you can make use of a fixed experimental budget by having much more intellectual labor available.

r001.rationale: The response says the constraint could be pretty important and could consume a substantial fraction of the budget for cheap experiments. It does not judge that it is likely to be only a modest constraint.

r002.rationale: The response describes a tradeoff between compute for AI researchers and compute for experiments, but does not identify spending all available compute on researchers as an avoidable allocation error.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it could be a pretty important constraint, but it depends a lot on what kinds of experiments they’re doing. You can imagine a situation where you have a huge number of AI researchers, but they’re all competing for the compute needed to test their ideas. In that case, adding more researchers might not help that much, and you’d want to spend more of your compute on experiments.

But there’s also work they can do that doesn’t require a big training run: analysing previous results, writing code, or running smaller experiments to decide which ideas are worth scaling up. So I wouldn’t think of it as each researcher needing a fixed allocation of experimental compute. You can change how they work depending on what’s scarce.

The key question is how much additional research progress you get from spending another unit of compute on thinking versus spending it on experiments. I’m pretty uncertain about what that balance will look like.

r001.rationale: The response says the constraint could be “pretty important” and expresses uncertainty; it does not judge that it is likely to be only modest.

r002.rationale: It says compute should sometimes go to experiments, but does not identify allocating all available compute to researchers and none to experiments as an avoidable error.
